_comment: Eight main screens aligned with the approved Figma wireframes. Educational content follows the revised learning journey.
title: Depth-First Search on a Binary Search Tree

screens.title: Welcome to the DFS Tutor
body: Learn Binary Search Trees and Depth-First Search through explanations, interactive visualisations and guided practice.
Discover how trees work, follow DFS step by step and check your understanding before the lecture.

screens.title: Binary Search Trees
body: A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where each node has at most two children.
Values smaller than a node belong in its left subtree. Larger values belong in its right subtree.
The top node is called the root. A node without children is called a leaf.
Try inserting 65 into the example tree and observe where it belongs.

options.text: One root with connected child nodes and no cycles
Nodes connected in a closed loop

questions.prompt: You push 1, then 2, then 3 onto a stack. Which value comes off first?

refreshers.trees: A tree contains connected nodes without cycles. The top node is the root. Nodes may have children, and nodes without children are leaves.
refreshers.stacks: A stack follows Last In, First Out (LIFO). The last value pushed onto the stack is the first value removed.

screens.title: Introduction to Depth-First Search
body: Depth-First Search explores one branch as deeply as possible before backtracking.
A stack keeps track of nodes that still need to be explored.
For left-first DFS, push the right child before the left child so that the left child is visited first.
DFS does not use the BST ordering rule to skip branches.
Pre-order records a node before its subtrees, in-order records it between its subtrees, and post-order records it after its subtrees.

screens.title: Interactive DFS Visualizer
body: Explore how Depth-First Search works on a Binary Search Tree.
Start by searching for 60. Follow the highlighted nodes and watch the stack change.
Use Previous, Next and Restart to follow the algorithm at your own pace.
Explore pre-order, in-order and post-order traversals, then experiment with inserting your own values.
screens.afterRun: DFS follows a traversal order. In-order traversal of a Binary Search Tree lists values in ascending order.

screens.title: Guided DFS Practice
body: Now it is your turn to practise Depth-First Search.
Practice 1: Predict which node will be visited next when searching for 55.
Practice 2: Write the in-order traversal of the example tree.
Use the available hints if you need help.

screens.title: Readiness Quiz
body: Answer six questions to check your understanding of Binary Search Trees and Depth-First Search.
After each answer, indicate how confident you are.
The quiz is for learning, not for marks.

screens.title: Feedback and Guided Review
body: Review any concepts you found difficult during the quiz.
**Binary Search Trees:** Remember that smaller values belong in the left subtree and larger values belong in the right subtree.
**Depth-First Search:** Explore one branch deeply before returning to another branch.
**Stacks:** The last node pushed is the first node popped. For left-first DFS, push right before left.
**Traversal orders:** Pre-order is root-left-right, in-order is left-root-right, and post-order is left-right-root.
**Try again:** Return to the DFS Visualizer, replay the worked example and practise predicting the next node.

screens.title: Learning Summary
body: **What you have learned**
- How Binary Search Trees organise values.
- How DFS explores a tree and backtracks.
- How a stack remembers pending nodes.
- How pre-order, in-order and post-order traversals differ.
**Think about these questions before your lecture:**
1. Why might a normal BST lookup find a value in fewer visits than DFS?
2. When might you explore a tree level by level instead of depth first?
You can revisit the lessons and practise again whenever you need to.
